sections.narration:
Welcome. Today we are exploring Your Personal Speaking Map and Continuing Plan. You have explored several tools. Some helped in particular moments, some were neutral and some still feel unfamiliar. You wonder which approach you are supposed to follow from now on.

In this session, we will choose a small current tool kit, link a tool to a real situation, and review and adjust your plan. I will explain the idea, show a visual example, and invite you to try it in a small experience of your own. You can ask me a question or switch to reading at any point. We will finish by choosing what, if anything, you want to take into a real conversation.

sections.narration:
You have explored several tools. Some helped in particular moments, some were neutral and some still feel unfamiliar. You wonder which approach you are supposed to follow from now on.

Selecting fewer tools for a period can make practice clearer. Choose one psychological approach and one body practice only if both serve your current goal. They can also be explored separately. Plan general speaking experiences so practice remains connected to life, rather than becoming only the rehearsal of techniques.

How do I know when to change the plan?

Choose a small review point and a few observations that matter. Ask whether the practice is usable, whether it serves a real situation and whether it increases or reduces unnecessary effort. Keep a useful practice, adjust a crowded one and leave unclear results open. The map is allowed to change. Its job is to help you choose the next part of your journey, not predict every future conversation.

sections.narration: For this next attempt, keep one clear purpose. Explain your small speaking map to your future self: the situation, one support or experiment, and how you will review it without turning the week into an exam. You can listen back if useful, or reflect without replaying. Changed, unchanged or uncertain experiences are all information.

sections.narration: This session is available at any point, not only after completing the catalogue. A map can begin with one tool and one situation. A change of plan can be a thoughtful response to experience. A changed, unchanged or uncertain experience is information, not a grade. You do not have to report relief for this attempt to count as exploration.

sections.narration: Save a seven-day plan with one focus, a few realistic speaking opportunities and one short review. Choose what to keep, change or explore next. During focused practice, you can deliberately explore this one tool. In an everyday conversation, give most of your attention to the message and the other person. A familiar support can be available if it helps; you do not have to monitor the tool throughout the exchange.
